card.tagline: A 1970s popular disco couple dance where partners bump hips to the beat.
card.profile: The Bump is a popular dance and music style introduced in the United States during the 1970s. In this couple dance, partners bump their hips or rear ends against each other to the rhythm of the music while otherwise avoiding physical touch. It gained widespread popularity through various disco and funk tracks in the mid-1970s and is considered by some to be a precursor to modern grinding.
card.insight: Introduced in the United States in the 1970s, the Bump features partners bumping hips or rear ends to the beat without otherwise touching.

card.profile_long: The Bump, also referred to as the hip bump due to its defining action, emerged as a popular dance form and music style in the United States during the 1970s. As a prominent feature of the era's disco and funk explosion, the dance involves two partners—generally one male and one female—who coordinate their movements to the beat of the song. Unlike many traditional partner dances that require continuous physical embrace, dancers executing the Bump typically do not touch each other except for the rhythmic contact of their hips or rear ends colliding in time with the music. In some instances, the choreography could take on a more suggestive character, with the female dancer bumping her hip against the male dancer's crotch. Because of this suggestive movement, the Bump is frequently cited as a historical precursor to the later, more controversial and erotic dance style known as grinding. The cultural footprint of the Bump extended far beyond American dance floors during the mid-1970s, propelled by a wave of charted singles across Europe and North America. Notable musical contributions came from funk and soul acts such as The Commodores, whose 1974 debut album Machine Gun featured a track titled 'The Bump', followed by a shortened version on their 1975 album Caught in the Act. Other major artists capitalized on the craze in 1975, including Kenny, Penny McLean with 'Lady Bump', Dooley Silverspoon with 'Bump Me Baby', and groups like The Bumpers, Black Buster, and Funky Family. The trend reached further mainstream milestones in 1977 when soul singer Joe Tex achieved a major international chart success with 'Ain't Gonna Bump No More (With No Big Fat Woman)', which reached high chart positions in both the United States and the United Kingdom and earned a gold certification in the US. Despite its massive commercial visibility during the 1970s disco era, detailed documentation regarding specific footwork, posture, costume design, and spatial formation remains sparse in historical sources, leaving gaps in the complete technical reconstruction of the dance beyond its core hip-bumping action.
